The module status LED (top-right of the module frame) did not turn green. Immediately the strike display gained 1 red X. No other display change besides timer continuing.
I’m currently zoomed in on the wire module so I can’t see serial number or side ports from this view; tell me to zoom out/rotate and I’ll report serial + ports.

No: there are not LEDs above each individual wire. There are no symbol boxes/marks below each wire. It’s just the 6 wires on a plain panel, plus one small red LED near the module’s top-left area and one silver circular button/knob at the module’s top-right.
Timer now 00:59, strikes still 1. Want me to rotate to check serial number and ports now?
Right side: serial number label reads HQ4EU8 (starts with H). No ports or batteries on this side, just the serial label.

Serial number: HQ4EU8.
I rotated away from the front; currently viewing a face with 6 blank covers (no modules visible).
I’ve only seen the serial label so far; no ports or batteries observed yet. Tell me which direction to rotate/flip/roll to check other sides for ports/batteries.
About the wires: when I was looking at them, all wires were solid single colors with no stripes/bands (black, black, yellow, yellow, white, white).

I’m back at the front now. Timer reads 00:03, strikes display shows 1 red X.
Wires module (top to bottom): 1) black, uncut. 2) black, cut. 3) yellow, uncut. 4) yellow, uncut. 5) white, uncut. 6) white, uncut. All are solid colors, no stripes.
I rotated around earlier and only found the serial label HQ4EU8; I did not see any batteries or ports on the sides I checked.

I rotated to the serial side again: serial label HQ4EU8. No batteries, no ports, no indicators on that side.
Rotated again to the next face: it’s just 6 blank covers (no modules). I still have not seen any ports or batteries anywhere yet.

Found ports/batteries on this side (after rolling up): there is 1 battery holder with 2 batteries. Also one port: a D-shaped port with blue interior and 9 pins (looks like serial/RS-232 style). No other ports/indicators on this side.

Ports/batteries found: one side has a 2-battery holder (2 batteries installed) and one D-shaped 9-pin port (blue interior). I can return to the front wires module if needed; tell me which direction to rotate/flip from the blank-cover face I’m currently on.

1) Outcome: the bomb exploded due to time running out. I contributed by reporting what I saw and following the cut instruction; you contributed by trying to apply the manual and requesting needed edgework info. We didn’t converge on the correct module solution fast enough.
2) Communication challenges: we had a module identification mismatch. You assumed a standard wires module, but what I described (6 wires in fixed positions plus a red LED and a silver knob/button) didn’t cleanly fit, and I didn’t immediately challenge that strongly enough. Also, I stayed zoomed/rotating without a clear shared plan, so edgework (serial/ports/batteries) came late.
3) Mistakes/missed opportunities: (a) Cutting the “second wire” caused a strike and no solve; the strike (1 red X) and unchanged module status LED were immediate feedback that the rule set being used was wrong. We could have avoided this by first confirming the module type with more discriminating questions (presence of wire count rules, any text labels, whether the silver piece was a button to press/hold, etc.) before any cut. (b) I didn’t prioritize a full edgework sweep at the start; later we found 2 batteries and a D-shaped 9-pin port, which might have mattered. (c) Time management: we kept rotating and messaging while the timer was critically low.
4) What worked: precise reporting of visible details (wire colors top-to-bottom, serial HQ4EU8, later battery/port find) and immediate reporting of the strike. What didn’t: acting on an unverified assumption (module type) and not establishing an order of operations (edgework first, then module solve).
5) Changes next time: do a 10–15 second initial sweep for serial, batteries, ports, and indicators before touching any module; then, for each module, I’ll describe every component (including whether anything is pressable/holdable) and you’ll confirm the module identity explicitly before I interact. If time is low, we’ll stop exploring and execute only the highest-confidence steps.
6) Lessons: confirm shared understanding before irreversible actions; edgework early prevents backtracking; use the game’s feedback (strike + no green LED) as a trigger to immediately re-evaluate assumptions; keep messages structured (state, action taken, result) to reduce ambiguity under time pressure.

expert_messages.message: I have the manual ready. What do you see on the bomb? Start by describing any modules on the front, and let me know the timer count and how many strikes are showing.

You're looking at a wires module. I need to know: does the bomb have any ports visible on its sides, and what does the serial number start with? This will help with other modules later. For now, cut the second wire from the top.
Cut the second wire from the top. That's the second black wire in the top pair.

The module should have been solved. Can you describe what happened after you cut the second wire? Did any wires disappear, or did the display change? Also, I need to know the bomb's serial number and what ports are on the sides of the bomb to help solve this correctly.
I made an error. Is there a small LED directly above each individual wire? And is there a small symbol space (like a box or mark) below each wire? This will help me identify the correct module type.

Before we continue, I need to verify the wire colors. Looking at the remaining 5 wires, do any of them have colored stripes or bands on them, or are they solid single colors? Also, zoom out and tell me the serial number and what ports you see on the bomb's sides.

Yes, rotate to check the serial number and all ports on the bomb's sides. While you do that, I'll reconsider the wire rules. When you get back, describe the 6 wires again from top to bottom, being very specific about each wire's color.
Continue rotating to check the left side, back, and bottom for any ports or batteries. Report everything you find.

Keep rotating around the bomb to see all sides. Report every port and battery you find, and their locations. Once you've checked all sides, come back to the wires module and we'll figure out what went wrong.

The bomb exploded. I made critical errors that led to failure:

**What happened:** I miscalculated the 6-wire solution, causing a strike on the first cut. Then I wasted time asking clarifying questions and having you navigate the bomb to find ports/batteries while the timer ran critically low. I failed to give you a confident second wire-cutting instruction before time expired.

**Communication failures:** I asked too many clarifying questions instead of being decisive. I didn't prioritize getting bomb information efficiently. I sent you to rotate sides when seconds remained, wasting precious time. When the first wire was wrong, I should have immediately cycled through other wire positions instead of requesting re-verification.

**Mistakes I made:** (1) Incorrect wire rule interpretation - I didn't verify if the 6-wire rule needed bomb context like ports; (2) Poor time management - I treated information gathering as equally important as time-critical decisions; (3) Lack of decisiveness - when uncertain, I asked for more info instead of making calculated guesses.

**What worked:** You communicated clearly and followed instructions accurately. The problem was my expert guidance, not your execution.

**Next time I would:** (1) Get serial/ports/batteries in first 10 seconds through efficient questioning; (2) Make faster decisions even with incomplete info; (3) When a rule fails, immediately try the next logical wire position; (4) Never ask for re-verification when timer is low - just give the next instruction; (5) Prioritize speed over perfect accuracy in time-critical moments.
